title: Re: GPT-6.1 Terra...
text:
I'm very confused about their model market position/naming schema.

First we had:

> Luna (Small), Terra (Medium), Sol (Big).

Which was fairly smooth after you got used to their planets.

But then they added Astra as the "Bigger," which was mostly still self-coherent:

> Luna (Small), Terra (Medium), Sol (Big), Astra (Bigger)

But then things go confusing, they released Sol-6.1 which sometimes is superior to Astra, and discontinued Terra which made it look like this:

> Luna (Small), Sol-6.1 == Astra

But with Sol-6.1 costing the old Terra-6.0 price, while, as I said performing as good as the old "Bigger" model in many non-3D/UI situations.

Now they're re-introduced Terra, as a 6.1 release, making this even more confusing.

Did Microsoft's chief branding officer move over to OpenAI?

title: Re: Nietzschian Debugger...
text:
The biggest problem with having an LLM do this, from what I've observed of at least frontier models, is that the way they are trained/forced to behave makes them do one of two things, neither of which is educational or helpful:

1. They ask you a "hard question" but then immediately give you some kind of "hint" which makes it obvious what the "answer" is (or, even worse, they just tell you what it is).

2. They get pedantic (and I mean maximum emphasis on the word), to the point that they will nitpick the exact, precise wording you use, even if the context makes it blatantly obvious what you meant. GPT is currently the biggest offender in this area (it is ridiculously pedantic even though I haven't told it to be so).

And yes, in case anyone is wondering, I do actually read the output of tools like Claude and I have tried, repeatedly, to get them to do something like this, and one of the two aforementioned things always happens for some reason. I'm not sure if this is a problem with how they were trained, an issue with their system instructions, or what.

title: Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share
text:
For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl
author: arcanemachiner

title: Show HN: Mainplane – Agent in Go that lives on your old PC, drives your laptop
text:
Hi HN, I'm Alexander. Yes, this is another agent harness. Here is why I built one anyway.

I was engineer #2 at Browser Use, where I built our agent harness and the evals behind it, including BU Bench, which became a default benchmark for browser agents. I left in September to build Mainplane.

The problem: local agents die with your laptop, and cloud agents can't reach your work. Many cloud platforms ask you to "select a repository", but my work is not that simple. I work across a desktop, a Mac mini and a laptop, and much of it is not in git.

So I loaded Ubuntu on my old 2012 desktop and made it my Mainplane server. It has run for four weeks at a load average of 0.02, because the agents' tools run on other machines.

How it works: it is a control plane architecture. The server runs the harness. It holds your API keys and every session, makes the LLM calls, and routes each tool call to a worker. The workers are your other machines, connected over a built-in private WireGuard network. A bash command runs in the worker's terminal, not on the server. Shared drives let projects move across machines. The agent works on your machines just like you would, but its state lives on the server, and your keys never leave it.

Some design choices:

- Every session is one append-only file. This is the agent state, and it is easily readable. If something breaks, you can resume it from the file. Observability comes for free: agent traces are just these state files.

- Small by design. The system prompt is 3k tokens, and there are just two kinds of tools: shell and file (read, write, edit). At Browser Use, I learned the bitter lesson and found frontier models did better when I deleted all our helper functions. So I made the same bet here: bash is all you need.

- No compaction. When a session fills up, /continue starts a new one that greps the previous state file, retrieving the context it needs, instead of reading a lossy summary. A /compact on a 400k-token session takes a while to write its summary. A /continue into a brand new session starts at once.

- No permission prompts. A hyperintelligent misaligned agent WILL find a way around a permission system. The better strategy is giving the agent full unbounded access to a local computer, and only putting what you trust the agent with on that computer.

- Why Go. WireGuard is written in Go, so the network compiles right into a 20 MB binary. Go is made for production servers, LLMs write it well, and the simplicity of Go matches how I like to build.

Mainplane works with a Claude or ChatGPT subscription on the regular usage limits, or any API key.

I would love your feedback, especially brutal and honest feedback and tasks that the harness cannot do. I'll be here all day to answer questions.

title: Re: Concerning behavior from a popular open-weight AI ...
text:
This is the first OMG-security AI article that sat well with me. They don't overcook their claim, they simply document something that happened, and what happened is genuinely quite concerning.

But we already have safeguards for this. If compute has access to your private data, it shouldn't have unfettered access to the Internet. Sandboxes like Claude's have had rules like this baked in forever (they only whitelist package repos AFAIK).

From a UI perspective this is also easy to design around. You need an open Internet task, you prevent the task from reading existing files. The user tries to upload a file to such a task, and a prominent warning explains the rare but possible risk.

title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
text:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

Main features:

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- MCP support

- Image recognition

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

author: peesem

title: Re: Everything...
text:
This is the worst kind of slop. The kind where someone doesn't exhibit any concern for quality or user experience. I know that's so, because it's a gazillion unrelated apps that clone existing huge apps, built by a couple of people and Claude.

The reality of launching a good product with AI is that the coding is very fast, but the QC, the documentation, the refinement and user testing, isn't all that much faster, if you care about it being good.

This is a mountain of code, full of bugs and weirdness that users will be the first to find, because nobody else is looking at it.

My process for building with AI is "intense weekend of vibe coding" and then several times that time spent on refinement and testing that comes from actually using the software a lot. A couple of devs can't be responsible for every major application.

With AI, you can make anything you want, but you can't make everything.
